name: Open Iceberg lakehouse
use_case: One copy of data, many engines
description: An open lakehouse stores every table once — as Apache Iceberg on cheap object storage — and lets any number of engines read and write the same tables through a shared catalog. Spark runs batch and ML jobs, Trino serves interactive SQL, Flink streams appends, and DuckDB pulls extracts, all against identical data with ACID guarantees. The catalog (REST-based: Polaris, Nessie, Glue, Unity) is the contract that makes this safe: every commit goes through it, so engines never trample each other. The payoff is engine independence — you pick the best tool per workload and swap vendors without moving a byte.
when_to_use: Choose this when more than one engine genuinely needs the same tables — Spark for ML, Trino or a warehouse for BI, Flink for streaming — and copying data between them is the pain you want to kill.
Open formats are a strategic requirement: avoiding vendor lock-in, surviving M&A heterogeneity, or negotiating leverage over warehouse pricing.
Data volumes make warehouse-native storage pricing hurt, and object storage plus open compute is meaningfully cheaper.
You want to adopt new engines (DuckDB, a faster query engine, an AI runtime) later without a migration project.
when_not_to_use: A single warehouse already serves every workload well — the catalog, maintenance, and multi-engine operations are pure overhead until a second engine actually arrives.
The team is small and wants managed simplicity; running compaction, snapshot expiry, and catalog infrastructure is real engineering work.
Workloads are sub-second operational serving — Iceberg scan latency is analytical, not transactional (8).
Data is small enough that a single-node stack (11) answers every question.

hot_spots.title: Catalog fragmentation
hot_spots.detail: Two engines writing through different catalogs to the same table corrupts state — one catalog must own every commit.

hot_spots.title: Table maintenance
hot_spots.detail: Nobody owns compaction, snapshot expiry, and orphan-file cleanup, and six months later every query is slow and storage triples.

hot_spots.title: Engine feature gaps
hot_spots.detail: Not every engine supports the same Iceberg spec level — an engine that can't read position deletes silently returns wrong rows.

hot_spots.title: Access control split
hot_spots.detail: Catalog-level grants and object-storage ACLs drift apart, leaving a path that bypasses table permissions.

evolution.reason: Feed the same Iceberg tables continuously with Flink when freshness requirements drop to minutes.
Scale the multi-engine lakehouse across domains with product ownership and contracts.

stages.name: Lake storage
stages.role: Durable object storage holding all table data and metadata files
stages.rationale: S3 is the reference target every Iceberg engine supports first; ADLS and GCS are the equivalents on their clouds, and MinIO gives the same API self-hosted.

stages.name: Table format
stages.role: Open table format providing ACID commits, schema evolution, and time travel over files
stages.rationale: Iceberg has the broadest multi-engine and multi-vendor support — the whole point of this architecture. Delta fits Databricks-first shops; Hudi fits upsert-heavy CDC lakes.

stages.name: Catalog
stages.role: The single commit authority every engine reads and writes through
stages.rationale: Polaris implements the Iceberg REST spec with vendor-neutral credential vending. Nessie adds git-like branching; Glue and Unity are the managed picks when you're anchored to one vendor.

stages.name: Batch + ML engine
stages.role: Heavy transforms, backfills, and ML feature computation over shared tables
stages.rationale: Spark has the deepest Iceberg integration for writes, MERGE, and maintenance procedures; EMR and Dataproc are its managed forms.

stages.name: Interactive SQL
stages.role: Low-latency SQL for BI and ad-hoc exploration over the same tables
stages.rationale: Trino reads Iceberg natively at interactive speed and federates when needed; Athena is its serverless AWS form, DuckDB covers laptop-scale pulls, and Snowflake can mount the same tables.

stages.name: Table maintenance
stages.role: Compaction, snapshot expiry, and orphan-file cleanup that keep tables fast
stages.rationale: Iceberg maintenance procedures run as Spark jobs; an orchestrator schedules them per table so performance never silently decays.
